questions.question: What is the core training task during LLM pre-training?
options: Predicting the next token given all previous tokens, repeated across massive amounts of text
Translating between exactly two specific languages
questions.explanation: Pre-training uses next-token prediction as its core objective. Grammar, facts, and reasoning patterns emerge as a side effect of getting very good at this single, simple-sounding task at massive scale.

questions.question: Why might a freshly pre-trained 'base model' respond to a question by continuing it with more text rather than directly answering it?
options: Base models are broken and unusable
Base models are trained purely on next-token prediction and haven't been specifically adapted to follow instructions or act as a helpful assistant
Base models can only output single words
Base models don't understand language at all
questions.explanation: Pre-training alone produces a model good at plausible text continuation, not one aligned to helpfully follow instructions — that alignment typically comes from a subsequent fine-tuning step.

questions.question: A team proposes pre-training their own foundation model from scratch to have full control. Which question best surfaces the real trade-off?
options: Can we start this project today without further discussion?
Given the scale of compute, data, and cost typically required for pre-training, would fine-tuning an existing pre-trained model address our actual underlying concern at far lower cost and risk?
Why do we need any training at all?
Can we skip pre-training and go straight to production?
questions.explanation: Pre-training from scratch is an extremely high-cost, high-risk undertaking realistic for only a small number of well-resourced organizations. Identifying the underlying concern (cost, privacy, capability) often reveals that fine-tuning or prompting an existing model addresses it far more practically.
